sources.quote: Pedagogical course with no general word-stress section (no other hits for 'stress'/'accent'). Only remark: 'To negate the Continuous, drop 'don and change the -a to -ataa. Note particularly that there is stress on the -at- ...'; 'Remember that the first a of -ataa is stressed and the aa is long.' Consistent with Stennes's stressed negative suffix (and Taylor's final accent in the negative past); otherwise silent.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'The accent is predominantly a stress accent, and, generally speaking, depends on the long vowels.' Disyllables: (1) if the first vowel is long or diphthongal it has the accent (sudu, ndi); (2) if two medial consonants or first vowel short, 'the accent is even' (nagge, puchu); (3) accent on the last syllable in the negative past (o warai) and nogas 'twenty'. Trisyllables: (1) long penult has the accent (lamido, rawandu); (2) short penult -> accent on the first vowel (karehi, derewol, o heniti; all trisyllabic derived verbs). 'In polysyllables the accent is free, but is usually on the penultima
